## Proof

Let $\Lambda_n = \mathbb{E}(S_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i$. By hypothesis $\Lambda_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$.

Since the $X_i$ are independent Poisson, $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Poi}(\Lambda_n)$. In particular:
- $\mathbb{E}(S_n) = \Lambda_n$,
- $\operatorname{Var}(S_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \Lambda_n$ (independence + Poisson variance equals its mean).

Consider $Y_n = \dfrac{S_n}{\mathbb{E}(S_n)} = \dfrac{S_n}{\Lambda_n}$. Then
$$\mathbb{E}(Y_n) = \frac{\Lambda_n}{\Lambda_n} = 1, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_n) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_n)}{\Lambda_n^2} = \frac{\Lambda_n}{\Lambda_n^2} = \frac{1}{\Lambda_n}.$$

For any $\varepsilon > 0$, by Chebyshev's inequality applied to $Y_n$ (which has mean $1$),
$$\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left|Y_n - 1\right| > \varepsilon\right) \le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)}{\varepsilon^2} = \frac{1}{\Lambda_n\,\varepsilon^2}.$$

Since $\Lambda_n \to \infty$, the right-hand side tends to $0$. Hence
$$\frac{S_n}{\mathbb{E}(S_n)} \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} 1.$$

The normalized sum converges in probability to $1$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
